title: What if the square is flipped over a slanting line?
description: The same labelled square is flipped over the line joining two opposite corners, and then over the horizontal middle line. Keeko doubts that corners on the line stay still.
teaching_notes: One idea: a point on the line stays, and a point off the line crosses to the matching place at the same distance. Watch for students who move every corner, even the ones sitting on the line.

source: For the same square ABCD (A top left, B top right, C bottom right, D bottom left): what if we reflect along the diagonal from A to C? Where do points A, B, C and D go? What if we reflect along the horizontal line of symmetry?
video_script.why: The child applies the same crossing rule to a slanting line and to the horizontal line, and sees which corners stay.
video_script.substitution: Keep the corners on the line where they are, and move each corner off the line to the matching place on the other side.
video_script.anchor: The same square with corners A at the top left, B at the top right, C at the bottom right and D at the bottom left, with a slanting dotted line from A to C and a horizontal dotted line through its middle
video_script.wrong_answer: every corner moves, even those on the line
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says every corner moves, even those on the line. A corner on the line has no other side to cross to, so it stays, and the idea is struck out.
video_script.payoff_line: A point on the line stays, and a point off it crosses to the matching place.

final_answer.value: Along diagonal AC: A and C stay, B and D swap. Along the horizontal line: A and D swap, B and C swap
final_answer.spoken: along the diagonal, eigh and C stay, and B and D swap places. Along the horizontal line, eigh and D swap places, and B and C swap places

maths_rules: Flipping a shape over a line is a reflection.
A line joining two opposite corners of a square is a diagonal.
A point on the line of symmetry stays where it is.
A point off the line goes to the matching point on the other side, at the same distance from the line.
For the diagonal AC, B and D are on opposite sides at the same distance, so they swap.
For the horizontal line, no corner is on the line, so the top corners swap with the bottom corners: A with D, and B with C.
video_script.design: One idea: stay on the line, cross off the line. Assumes the child has seen the vertical reflection of the same square. The labelled square stays on the board from the hook to the end.

<bookmark mark='cross'/>Eigh lands where D was, and B lands where C was. The bottom corners go up in the same way.
